\chapter{Asking Someone's Age}
\label{ch:hi-asking-age}
\hlchaptermodality{19}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can ask someone's age in Hindi and give my own in the belonging-to-years shape Hindi uses.}

Ask \hi{तुम} \hi{कितने} \hi{साल} \hi{के} \hi{हो}? and answer \hi{मैं} \hi{बीस} \hi{साल} \hi{का} \hi{हूँ}, with \hi{के}/\hi{का} carrying the 'belonging to' work.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[\hi{उम्र}]{\hi{उम्र} — the same word as Arabic}

\label{lesson:HI-C19-umr}



\begin{quote}
You just met Arabic's \emph{ʿumr}. Hindi's everyday word for \textquotedblleft{}age\textquotedblright{} is the \textbf{exact same word}, carried through Persian.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know — \hi{उम्र} — a Perso-Arabic loan, and a native alternative}
\textbf{\hi{उम्र}} (\emph{umr}) = \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{age}\textquotedblright{} — this is \textbf{Arabic's ʿumr}, borrowed into Hindi through Persian, and it's the everyday, colloquial word most Hindi speakers use. Hindi also has a fully \textbf{native Sanskrit} alternative, \textbf{\hi{आयु}} (\emph{āyu}, \textquotedblleft{}age, lifespan\textquotedblright{}), which feels more formal or literary — a register split you've now seen several times (compare Kannada's Sanskrit-tatsama \emph{madhyāhna} vs. Tamil's native words for the same concepts, just flipped here: the \textbf{borrowed} word is the everyday one, the \textbf{native} word is the formal one).

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textquotedblleft{}umr\textquotedblright{} — age, same word as Arabic's ʿumr
  \item \emph{Contrast:} everyday \emph{umr} · formal/literary \emph{āyu}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What language does Hindi's \textbf{\hi{उम्र}} come from, and what's the native Sanskrit alternative? (\textbf{Arabic} \emph{ʿumr}, via Persian; native alternative is \textbf{\hi{आयु}}, \emph{āyu}.) Which one is ordinary conversational Hindi? (\textbf{Umr}.) Next: use a genitive marker to say how many years someone belongs to.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kitne sāl ke ho?]{\hi{कितने} \hi{साल} \hi{के} \hi{हो}? — belonging to so many years}

\label{lesson:HI-C19-age-grammar}



\begin{quote}
Languages do not agree on whether age is something you have, are, were born with, or state without a verb. Hindi gives the idea a fifth shape.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know — The two sentences}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\hi{तुम} \hi{कितने} \hi{साल} \hi{के} \hi{हो}?} — \textquotedblleft{}How old are you?\textquotedblright{} (informal), literally \textquotedblleft{}you, \textbf{of how many years, are}?\textquotedblright{} (\emph{tum kitne sāl ke ho?})
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\hi{मैं} \hi{बीस} \hi{साल} \hi{का} \hi{हूँ।}} — \textquotedblleft{}I am twenty years old,\textquotedblright{} literally \textquotedblleft{}I {[}am one{]} \textbf{belonging to twenty years}.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{maiṅ bīs sāl kā hūṅ.})
\end{quote}

\textbf{\hi{के}/\hi{का}} (\emph{ke/kā}) is Hindi's \textbf{genitive postposition}, \textquotedblleft{}of, belonging to.\textquotedblright{} The same marker family handles possession elsewhere: \emph{merā ghar}, \textquotedblleft{}my house.\textquotedblright{}

So Hindi does not copy Romance's \textquotedblleft{}I \textbf{have} years,\textquotedblright{} Germanic's simple \textquotedblleft{}I \textbf{am} {[}a number{]},\textquotedblright{} Latin's \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{born} + N years,\textquotedblright{} or Arabic's verbless \textquotedblleft{}my age {[}is{]} N.\textquotedblright{} It says \textquotedblleft{}I am {[}one{]} \textbf{belonging to} N years,\textquotedblright{} with a genitive marker plus \textbf{\hi{होना}} (\emph{honā}, \textquotedblleft{}to be\textquotedblright{}).

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textquotedblleft{}tum kitne sāl ke ho?\textquotedblright{} — how old are you?
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textquotedblleft{}maiṅ bīs sāl kā hūṅ\textquotedblright{} — I belong to twenty years
  \item \emph{Point to:} \textbf{ke/kā} — the genitive, \textquotedblleft{}of/belonging to\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \textbf{\hi{के}/\hi{का}} mark? (A \textbf{genitive/possessive} relationship.) Does Hindi use Romance \textquotedblleft{}have,\textquotedblright{} simple Germanic \textquotedblleft{}be,\textquotedblright{} Latin \textquotedblleft{}born,\textquotedblright{} or Arabic's verbless sentence? (\textbf{None}: it says \textquotedblleft{}belonging to N years\textquotedblright{} + \emph{honā}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
